question_bank.stem: In the travel-booking example, where should a user's first name live if the agent needs it frequently in later turns?

options.text: In archival memory, because any personal fact should be treated as cold storage by default.
Inside the payment tool, because identity facts belong only in external APIs rather than the agent state.
In working memory, because it is a frequently needed fact that should be fast to retrieve.
Inside the system prompt, because prompts are the only valid place to keep conversational user information.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture distinguishes fast-access working memory from slower archival memory for facts used more frequently.

source_ref.evidence_span: is not every memory needs to be fast to access.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Travel Booking AI Agent slide shows prompts, context management, core memory, archival memory, and tools around the agent box.

question_bank.stem: Why did the lecture avoid putting every remembered fact into fast-access memory?

options.text: Because fast-access memory automatically overwrites user facts after each turn, so long-term recall becomes impossible.
Because fast-access memory can only store tool outputs and cannot store anything learned from conversation.
Because fast-access memory removes the need for prompts, which would make the travel-agent example unrealistic.
Because retrieving all memory on every turn can add cost and latency, so only frequently needed facts should stay in the fast path.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture notes that not every memory needs fast access and that indiscriminate retrieval can be costly.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Travel-agent architecture discussion continues while the instructor explains why every-memory retrieval can slow the system.

question_bank.stem: Which pair best matches the lecture's distinction between tools and resources?

options.text: A flight-search API is a tool, whereas a CRM datastore that the agent reads is a resource.
A CRM datastore is a tool, whereas a flight-search API is a resource.
A payment API and a weather API are both resources, because tools cannot make external calls.
A vector database and a system prompt are both tools, because each can change the final answer.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture treats APIs as tools and readable data stores such as a CRM as resources.

source_ref.evidence_span: The tools can include APIs like a flight search

frame_evidence.visual_description: Travel Booking AI Agent slide lists tool APIs such as flight search, hotel booking, weather, and payment next to the agent diagram.

question_bank.stem: A team wants one interface layer between the agent and many external endpoints instead of hard-coding every integration. Which concept from the lecture best fits?

options.text: Few-shot prompting, which turns every endpoint into an in-context example that no longer needs an API.
Model Context Protocol, which provides a middle layer so the agent can talk to tools or data endpoints more systematically.
Archival memory, which stores the external services so the agent never has to authenticate with them again.
Prompt chaining, which replaces all protocols by serializing each API call as another text-only prompt.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture introduces MCP as a protocol layer between agents and endpoints instead of one-off integrations.

source_ref.evidence_span: You probably have heard the term MCP or model context protocol

frame_evidence.visual_description: Later travel-agent discussion introduces MCP as an architectural middle layer between the agent and external systems.

question_bank.stem: Which design reflects the most autonomous end of the lecture's autonomy spectrum?

options.text: The agent follows hard-coded steps and hard-coded tools with no discretion about sequence or usage.
The agent follows hard-coded tools and must ask a human to approve each single prompt before execution.
The agent decides the steps itself and can even create tools or code when needed.
The agent uses only archival memory and no tools, so autonomy is defined entirely by memory depth.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture presents increasing autonomy from hard-coded steps to systems that decide steps and may create tools.
